text:
A: Hello! Hi! You can hear me okay?
B: Hi! Yeah, I can hear you. I'm Riya.
A: Riya, lovely name. I'm Agnieszka, but is difficult, you can say Aga. Sorry, my English, is not perfect.
B: No, honestly, your English is fine. Agnieszka. Did I say that right?
A: Yes! Very good. Two people today say my name properly, I'm so happy. How are you, you are okay?
B: Yeah, good thanks! Bit tired, I've got uni stuff, but good. How are you?
A: I'm okay, bit knackered, I start work six this morning. I am cleaner, offices and a GP surgery in Southampton. You are student?
B: Yeah, final year, business management at Queen Mary. And I work on reception at a dentist's in Stratford, like two days a week.
A: Oh, reception! I love the reception girls at my surgery, we always talk in the morning, I know all their birthdays. Is very busy there, always people waiting, always phone ringing.
B: Oh my god, yeah, the phone. And my dentist is always like twenty minutes behind, so I'm just sat there smiling at everyone, like, won't be long!
A: Won't be long! Yes, they say this also. You know, when I saw your picture, I think, oh, she looks like my daughter Natalia. The hair, the makeup, the eyes like this, with the line.
B: Aw, that's so sweet! How old is she?
A: Twenty-one. She moved out last year, with boyfriend, to Eastleigh. But she comes every Sunday for dinner, I make rosół, chicken soup, and she takes food home in boxes.
B: No way, that's literally me! I go back to my mum's in Harrow most Sundays and I always come home with, like, five tubs of food. And my laundry, if I'm honest.
A: The laundry also! Natalia, the same, she brings the bag. What your mum cooks?
B: She's Gujarati, so like thepla, which is kind of a flatbread with spices, and undhiyu, which is this veg thing. It's amazing. I can do a basic dal, but it's not the same.
A: Is never the same as mum. I make pierogi, big batches, maybe two hundred, and I freeze. Saturday I make with Natalia, she does the folding, I do the dough. Is nice, we talk, you know, like before.
B: That's actually so cute. Do you miss her being at home?
A: Erm, yes. Sort of. More than I tell her. Now is only my husband and my son, and my son, he don't talk, only phone and PlayStation. You live with your family?
B: No, I live with my boyfriend, in Leyton. We moved in like eight months ago, above a dry cleaner's. They start the machines at seven every morning.
A: Seven! I am already at work, ha. Your mum, she is happy you live with boyfriend?
B: Erm, she's fine. My aunties don't, like, fully know yet. So, you know. It's a whole thing.
A: Ah, the aunties. In Poland also, the aunties know everything about everybody. My mum calls me, she tells me who is getting married, who is pregnant, from people I don't remember!
B: Oh my god, that's my family group chat. Every day someone's cousin's engaged.
A: Exactly! So what you do after university? You have plan?
B: Kind of. Something in marketing, maybe for a beauty brand. I'm gonna sort it after my dissertation. That's what I keep saying, anyway.
A: You will be fine, you are friendly girl, people like this. Is most important, I think.
B: Aw, thank you. You're making me feel better about it, honestly.
A: Oh, the timer! Is finishing already?
B: I think so. It was so nice talking to you!
A: You too, lovely! Good luck with the university, bye bye!
